lessons.title: Clean, dry hands
lessons.text: CDC describes washing hands with soap and water, then drying them completely with a clean cloth before touching lenses.

reference.quote:
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water before handling lenses.
Dry hands completely with a clean cloth before touching lenses.

lessons.title: Keep lenses away from water
lessons.text: CDC says to keep contact lenses away from all water and remove them before swimming or showering.

reference.quote:
Keep contact lenses away from all water
Remove before swimming or showering to prevent germ exposure.

lessons.title: Fresh solution, not topping off
lessons.text: FDA distinguishes fresh solution from used solution: discard leftovers rather than topping off or reusing them.

reference.quote: Do not “top-off” the solutions in your case. Always discard all of the leftover contact lens solution after each use. Never reuse any lens solution.

lessons.title: The case needs care too
lessons.text: CDC describes rubbing and rinsing the case with solution, then storing it upside down with the caps off after each use.

reference.quote:
Take care of your contact lens case
Clean case with solution by rubbing and rinsing.
Store case upside down with caps off after each use.

lessons.title: Saline is not a disinfectant
lessons.text: Saline and disinfecting solutions have different roles. CDC states that saline does not disinfect contact lenses.

reference.quote: Saline solution does not disinfect contact lenses.

lessons.title: Peroxide: follow the product label
lessons.text: FDA says peroxide neutralization must finish before lenses go on the eyes. The required soaking time is on the product labeling; this lesson does not supply a universal time.

reference.quote: Always soak your contacts in the hydrogen peroxide solution for the required length of time indicated on the labeling. The neutralizing process must finish before you place your contacts on your eyes.

lessons.title: Single-use means a new pair
lessons.text: NEI describes single-use lenses as worn for one day and then discarded at night, with a new pair the next day. This describes that lens type, not a change to your prescribed schedule.

reference.quote: You wear single-use contact lenses for one day, then throw them away at night. The next day, you put in a brand new pair. You don’t need to clean or disinfect single-use lenses.

lessons.title: Check expiration and discard dates
lessons.text: FDA says not to use contact lens solutions beyond their expiration or discard date. Check the product label rather than using a generic duration from an app.

reference.quote: Do not use contact lens solutions that have gone beyond the expiration or discard date.

questions.prompt: According to CDC, what comes before handling lenses?

options.text: Wash with soap and water, then dry hands completely with a clean cloth
Only rinse fingertips
Skip washing if hands look clean

questions.explanation: CDC includes both washing and complete drying before touching lenses.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches CDC's water guidance?

options.text: Swimming water is an exception
Remove lenses before swimming or showering
Only sea water needs to be avoided

questions.explanation: CDC says all water, including swimming and showering.

questions.prompt: What does FDA say about leftover solution?

options.text: Keep it and add fresh solution
Reuse it if it looks clear
Discard it; do not reuse or top off

questions.explanation: FDA explicitly says to discard leftovers and never reuse lens solution.

questions.prompt: How does CDC describe storing the cleaned case?

options.text: Upside down with caps off
Full of used solution
Closed while still dirty

questions.explanation: CDC describes rubbing and rinsing with solution, then upside-down storage with caps off.

options.text: Yes, any saline disinfects
No, saline does not disinfect lenses
Only if the saline looks clear

questions.explanation: CDC states that saline solution does not disinfect contact lenses.

questions.prompt: Where does FDA say to find peroxide's required soaking time?

options.text: A single universal time for all products
The color of the solution
The product labeling; neutralization must finish

questions.explanation: Required time comes from the labeling, and neutralization must finish before lenses are placed on the eyes.

questions.prompt: How does NEI describe single-use lenses?

options.text: One day, discard at night, new pair the next day
Clean them to reuse indefinitely
Share them after rinsing

questions.explanation: NEI distinguishes single-use from reusable lenses; this is not a new prescribed schedule.

questions.prompt: Which dates does FDA say matter for solution?

options.text: Only the purchase date
Expiration or discard date
Dates do not matter if the bottle is full

questions.explanation: FDA says not to use solution past its expiration or discard date.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches FDA's solution rule?

options.text: Used solution becomes fresh when mixed
Leftovers are reusable once
Never reuse lens solution

questions.explanation: FDA's wording is explicit: never reuse any lens solution.

questions.prompt: What must finish before peroxide-treated lenses go on the eyes?

options.text: The neutralizing process specified by the label
Only opening the case
No process needs to finish

questions.explanation: FDA says the neutralizing process must finish; follow all product labeling instructions.
